title: Knowledge Check 9: Lessons 65-72
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 65-72 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A team is preparing a supervised fine-tuning set to install a specific behavior. Which data choice gives the model the best chance of learning it?
options: A small set of realistic examples drawn from production prompts, paired with desired outputs.
A large set of scraped examples, on the theory that more data always improves a tune.
A set generated entirely by a weaker model so every example shares one uniform style.
A single long document describing the desired behavior in prose rather than in example pairs.
questions.explanation: The tuned model is bounded by the quality of its examples, so a small, clean, representative set paired with human ground truth beats a large noisy one. Quantity alone does not teach a behavior the examples never demonstrate.

questions.question: Full fine-tuning updates every weight in a large model. What does low-rank adaptation do instead to make the adaptation affordable?
options: It retrains the entire model on a smaller slice of the data at each step.
It removes most layers from the model so fewer weights exist to update.
It freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank update matrices.
It replaces the base model with a fixed lookup table of stored responses.
questions.explanation: Low-rank adaptation holds the original weights fixed and learns a compact update expressed as the product of two much smaller matrices. Because those matrices carry far fewer parameters, the training fits on modest hardware.

questions.question: A team wants the evaluation of a fine-tune to be trustworthy. Which practice supports that goal?
options: Judging the tune by how smoothly the training run progressed and how low its training loss fell.
Reusing a few evaluation examples during training so the model recognizes them and scores well.
Relying on the platform's automated safety checks as the only measure of quality.
Comparing the tuned model to the base model on a held-out set kept out of training.
questions.explanation: Evaluation has to be set up before training and must rely on a held-out set that never enters the data, with the tuned model compared to the base model on that same set. Training loss and a smooth run say nothing about whether the model generalizes.

questions.question: How does a multimodal model connect a word in a prompt to the region of an image it refers to?
options: Cross-attention in a shared embedding space that binds words to image regions.
A separate OCR pass that turns the image into text before the language model runs.
A captioning step that replaces the image with a written description of it first.
The language model is discarded so only the vision encoder produces the answer.
questions.explanation: Each modality is encoded, projected into one shared embedding space, then fused by cross-attention, which lets one modality selectively attend to parts of another. That is what binds a word to the pixels it names.

questions.question: An agent only needs the total printed on a clean, large-print receipt. What perception choice follows from how vision is billed?
options: Send the image at high detail, since maximum resolution is always the safest read.
Use low detail, since a simple read does not need the extra tile tokens.
Skip vision entirely, since a printed total can be inferred from context.
Send one image per field, so each value gets its own dedicated model pass.
questions.explanation: An image is billed as base tokens plus, at higher detail, a stack of tile tokens, so a task that needs only a simple read should use low detail. The skill is buying only the resolution the task requires.

questions.question: An agent must reproduce every cell of a dense table exactly for downstream processing. Which approach fits the task?
options: A general vision model reading the page at high detail in a single pass.
A text-only model given a short summary of the table's contents.
A specialized extraction pipeline tuned for exact table structure.
A general model asked to describe the table's overall meaning in prose.
questions.explanation: Flexible in-context reasoning suits a general multimodal model, but exact, high-volume reproduction of tables and charts is where a specialized extractor wins on accuracy and speed. The choice is a routing decision per task, not one tool for everything.

questions.question: Why is a voice agent commonly built as a speech-to-text, language model, and text-to-speech chain?
options: Because the reasoning and tool use happen in the model's text token space.
Because speech-to-speech models cannot produce any natural-sounding output.
Because this chain is the only way to stay under any latency target at all.
Because the speech components, not the model, perform the reasoning and tool use.
questions.explanation: The intelligence lives in the language model, which expects text, so the speech components act as an input and output layer that converts audio into tokens and back. The reasoning and tools are unchanged from a text agent.

questions.question: A voice agent feels sluggish even though each component is individually fast. What change brings the first response audio sooner?
options: Wait for the user to finish speaking before transcribing any of the audio.
Use a larger language model so each response is more accurate and reliable.
Increase the silence timeout so the agent waits longer before replying.
Stream partial transcripts into the model and partial text into synthesis.
questions.explanation: The latency budget closes only when stages overlap: recognition emits words while the user speaks, the model is primed on the partial transcript, and synthesis speaks the first clause early. What matters is time to first audio, not total completion.

questions.question: While the agent reads a long explanation, a caller says "uh-huh" to show they are listening. How should a well-designed interruption policy treat that input?
options: As a correction that should immediately cancel the agent's audio.
As noise that should be logged but never acted on at all.
As a backchannel that should not cancel the agent's audio.
As a new request that should redirect the whole conversation.
questions.explanation: Interruption handling is a policy, not a toggle: a listening sound like uh-huh is a backchannel that should usually not stop playback, while a true correction should. A false interruption that quits for a backchannel is more damaging than a missed one.

questions.question: What structural property of a computer-use agent makes it possible to place guardrails between the model and the real world?
options: The model returns a proposed action that a control layer in your code performs.
The model performs each mouse and keyboard action directly on the screen itself.
The model is prevented from reading any of the page content it might later act on.
The agent only runs on pages that contain no visual elements at all.
questions.explanation: The model only proposes; your control layer decides whether to carry the action out. That separation is where guardrails, approval gates, and allowlists live, so the model never touches the machine directly.

questions.question: An agent struggles on a JavaScript-heavy page where the page structure is noisy but the screen is clear. Which approach fits best?
options: Use only the accessibility tree, since it always reflects everything on the page.
Use only full screenshots, since the structured signal can never help on any page.
Use the structured signal, falling back to screenshots when it runs out.
Disable the step cap so the agent can keep retrying the same click forever.
questions.explanation: The hybrid approach defaults to the cheap structured signal, such as the accessibility tree or DOM, and falls back to screenshots on visual or noisy pages. Routing per task beats committing to a single way of seeing.

questions.question: Why is browser automation more exposed to prompt injection than a tool call you wrote yourself?
options: Browsers automatically strip all embedded text out of a page before a model can read it.
The page content the agent must read can itself carry hidden instructions.
Injected instructions can only ever change a chat answer and never a real action.
Web pages are always authored by the same user who asked the agent to visit them.
questions.explanation: A tool call has a defined shape you control, but a browsing agent must read the web, and the content it reads is the same channel an attacker can use to give it orders. That is why its guardrails assume content is untrusted rather than relying on the model to ignore attacks.

questions.question: What reframes the build-versus-buy decision for an agent framework most usefully?
options: Decide once whether to build every layer or rent every layer, with no mixing.
Park orchestration deliberately, buy commodities, and build your own domain logic.
Pick whichever path has the lowest price at signup, since exit cost is unknowable.
Always build every layer yourself, because any framework you adopt is unauditable.
questions.explanation: The real question is which layer is your product and which is a commodity: buy the foundation model and standard connectors, build the domain logic competitors cannot copy, and choose orchestration knowingly. Domain logic is the one layer where building is consistently justified.

questions.question: Why is a managed platform generally the hardest path to leave?
options: Because the vendor publishes its orchestration code openly for anyone to reuse.
Because nothing you build on it ever touches your own data or systems.
Because you never own the state, routing, or code that runs your loop.
Because managed platforms can never ship a working demo quickly.
questions.explanation: Leaving a managed platform means reimplementing orchestration you never wrote and porting state you never saw, so the convenience that sped up onboarding is paid back on exit. The general rule is that the faster something lets you ship, the more it costs to leave.

questions.question: What does adopting an open standard for tool and data integrations do for the cost of switching frameworks later?
options: It locks integrations to one framework, so switching requires rebuilding every connector.
It removes the need for any orchestration layer in the first place.
It makes the standard's governance controlled by a single vendor you depend on.
It makes integrations portable, so they survive a change of framework or model.
questions.explanation: Exposing a capability once as a standard server lets any compatible application use it, collapsing the integration matrix so the most expensive part of switching, rebuilding every connector, is avoided. The standard does not make leaving free, but it keeps the connections portable.

questions.question: What distinguishes a workflow from an agent in how an agentic system is built?
options: A workflow fixes the path in code, while an agent lets the model choose its steps.
A workflow runs on a stronger underlying model, while an agent must use a weaker one.
A workflow never calls any tools, while an agent always calls at least one tool.
A workflow always runs locally, while an agent must always run in the cloud.
questions.explanation: The difference is not model capability but who owns the decision of what happens next. In a workflow the code fixes the path; in an agent the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use.

questions.question: Which task is the right fit for giving a model autonomy rather than fixing the path in code?
options: A task whose steps and branches can all be confidently written down well in advance.
A task where the route cannot be predicted and the goal is the contract.
A task where every input falls into one of a few known categories.
A task whose success can never be checked by any automated means.
questions.explanation: Autonomy earns its place only where orchestration cannot reach: open-ended work where the number of steps is hard to predict and you can trust the model within guardrails. If the steps or branches can be enumerated, a workflow is the more reliable, cheaper choice.

questions.question: Most of a system is predictable, but one step depends on free-form input the team cannot enumerate. What design fits?
options: Make the whole system one autonomous agent, since any open-ended part forces full autonomy.
Give the model autonomy over the predictable steps and fix only the free-form step in code.
Orchestrate the predictable steps and give only the free-form step a bounded agent.
Leave the system unbuilt, since one unpredictable step makes it unreliable.
questions.explanation: The through-line is to maximize determinism where the task allows it and spend autonomy only on the open-ended residue, bounded by a step cap, a small tool palette, and a check on its output. Production systems almost always land in the middle.

questions.question: Why are the control plane and the data plane kept separate in an agent platform?
options: Because control governs and stays stable, while data executes and scales fast.
Because the data plane is only needed when the platform happens to store a database.
Because the two planes must run on identical hardware to avoid added latency.
Because small deployments do not need a control plane at all.
questions.explanation: They change at different speeds and answer to different teams: policy, identity, and audit must stay stable, while throughput, latency, and tool calls must scale. Merging them means a policy change risks the data path and a data-path change risks governance.

questions.question: In a modern serving plane, where do an agent's memory, loop, and tool calls live?
options: Inside the model, which retains them across requests between turns.
In a separate harness, because the model is a stateless service.
In the data plane, which stores them as governed context.
In the gateway, which replays them on every request.
questions.explanation: The serving plane treats the model as a stateless service: it takes a prompt, returns a completion, and forgets. The loop, memory, context window, and tool calls live in the harness, which is what lets you swap the model without rewriting the agent.

questions.question: Why should a platform's control plane be portable and attached to the asset rather than to one cloud's native tooling?
options: Because native cloud governance is always slower than a custom control plane.
Because no cloud vendor offers any governance tooling for agents at all.
Because asset-aware governance is required by law in every jurisdiction.
Because governance written in one cloud's schema cannot move to another.
questions.explanation: Governance expressed in a vendor's proprietary constructs is non-transferable: a multi-cloud portfolio needs separate stacks in separate policy languages, and the tooling that looked free at signup becomes the lock-in at exit. Governing by what the asset is keeps policy portable.

questions.question: Why is the gateway the right place to enforce policy in an agent platform?
options: Because every request crosses it, so it can stop an action early.
Because it is the only component able to run the language model.
Because it stores all of the agent's long-term memory between its sessions.
Because it replaces the policy engine entirely, so no decision layer is needed.
questions.explanation: Policy written only in a design document stops nothing; it takes effect where traffic actually flows. Every agent request passes through the gateway, so it can authenticate the caller and halt an action before it reaches a model or tool.

questions.question: How are enforcement and decision-making divided between the gateway and the policy engine?
options: The gateway makes every allow or deny decision itself from hardcoded rules.
The policy engine sits in the request path and enforces what the gateway decides.
The gateway enforces; the policy engine evaluates and returns the decision.
Both are optional, since policy can live inside each agent's prompt.
questions.explanation: Separating the enforcement point from the decision point keeps the enforcement code simple and stable while the policy changes on its own. The gateway stays in the traffic path as the enforcer, and the policy engine returns the allow or deny decision.

questions.question: What does a default-deny policy rule accomplish in a policy layer built to govern agent actions?
options: It allows any action unless a policy explicitly forbids it.
It forbids any action unless a policy explicitly allows it.
It logs every action but blocks none of them at runtime.
It defers every decision to the agent's own prompt instructions.
questions.explanation: Default deny makes the safe path the default: an action is refused unless a policy explicitly permits it, and a forbid-wins rule means one denial stands even if another policy allows. That is the right bias when the actor is an agent you cannot fully predict.
